sbh2.5:1.3: Asanga gives a **six-element** scheme rather than the four-great-element analysis dominant in the Theravada tradition. The six adds space (*ākāśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), giving a complete decomposition of the embodied person, not just the physical body. This follows MN 140 (Dhātuvibhaṅga) and MN 62 (Mahā-Rāhulovāda) rather than VSM Ch 11.
sbh2.5:2.3: *upādatta* — 'taken up, appropriated' — is technical. It marks the element-instance that has become *part of a being* through the appropriation-process of consciousness. The body's hard parts are *upādatta* earth; external rocks are not. The practice is to see that, whether or not upādatta, it is still earth.
sbh2.5:2.6: Same body-parts list as the *aśubhā* section, but here framed as instances of the earth element rather than objects of disgust. A key Yogācāra point: the same observation can serve as either *aśubhā* (antidote to lust) or *dhātu-prabheda* (antidote to pride), depending on how it is held.
sbh2.5:4.5: Four functions of inward fire enumerated: general bodily warmth (*ātapyate*), feverish heat (*saṁtapyate*), burning sensation (*paritapyate*), and digestive heat (*paripākaṁ gacchati*). The last function is the standard *pakkācchaka* of the Pali commentaries.
sbh2.5:5.10: *vāyv-aṣṭhīlā* / *vātāṣṭhīlā* — 'wind-stretching' or 'knotty winds' (uncertain). Likely refers to localized rigidity or knotted winds in Indian medical analysis.
sbh2.5:5.11: *kṣuraka-pippalaka-śastrakā* — 'razor-pippal-blade winds.' Hapax legomenon; the precise referent is uncertain. Translated conjecturally as sharp, stabbing pains attributed to disturbed wind.
sbh2.5:5.23: *nirupādāno nirgacchati* — 'it goes on without appropriation.' The great wind that fells trees and walls is described as *not* appropriated — silently underscoring the elemental point: the great wind is the same kind of thing as the breath in your nose; one is *upādatta*, the other is not, but the element is the same.
sbh2.5:7.3: The line does not introduce a full later Yogācāra eight-consciousness scheme. After listing the six sense-consciousnesses, it glosses the consciousness element more generally as *citta* and *mano-vijñāna*. Treat this as a compact consciousness-element definition, not as a separate doctrinal taxonomy of *citta/manas/vijñāna*.
sbh2.5:8.1: *Māna-carita* is kept as conceit-conduct, matching the conduct-label style in the surrounding practice chapters. *Piṇḍa-saṁjñā* is the perception of the body as one solid thing, the implicit 'this is me' that conceit hooks into. *Vibhāvayati* means 'dispels, breaks down' this lump-perception. Once the body is perceived as six elements in their inward and outward forms, there is no unified entity to claim ownership of.
sbh2.5:8.2: The practice has a useful side-effect: *aśubha-saṁjñā* arises naturally as well. *Dhātu-prabheda* is dual-purpose — primary antidote to pride, secondary antidote to lust. A practitioner whose primary issue is pride but who also struggles with attraction can use this practice as covering both grounds.
